questions.prompt: What best describes the pulse of a piece?
questions.explanation: A pulse provides a regular timing reference; the rhythm can change around it.
questions.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
questions.label: Find a steady pulse

questions.prompt: In 4/4 with a quarter-note beat, how long is a half note?
questions.explanation: A half note is two quarter-note beats in this example.

questions.prompt: Which word describes how high or low a note sounds?
questions.explanation: Pitch concerns high and low; tempo concerns speed and duration concerns length.
questions.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
questions.label: Follow a pitch shape

questions.prompt: How many quarter-note beats fit in two complete bars of 4/4?
questions.explanation: Each bar has four quarter-note beats, giving eight across two bars.

questions.label: Shape a small phrase

questions.prompt: A pattern becomes uneven at a fast tempo. What is a useful next practice step?
options: Slow down and isolate the difficult part

recall_questions.prompt: You clap different patterns while tapping evenly. What is your foot keeping?
recall_questions.explanation: The even tapping maintains the pulse while your clapping creates a rhythm.
recall_questions.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
recall_questions.label: Find a steady pulse

recall_questions.prompt: How many quarter-note beats are left after a half note in one 4/4 bar?
recall_questions.explanation: The bar holds four quarter-note beats, so four minus two leaves two.
recall_questions.hint: Break the idea into one small step.

recall_questions.prompt: A melody moves from C up to D up to E in the same register. What is its contour?
recall_questions.explanation: The pitches rise. Rising pitch does not imply rising loudness.
recall_questions.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
recall_questions.label: Follow a pitch shape

recall_questions.prompt: A three-bar 4/4 pattern has how many quarter-note beats in total?
recall_questions.explanation: Three bars of four quarter-note beats give twelve beats.
recall_questions.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
recall_questions.label: Shape a small phrase

recall_questions.prompt: Which practice goal is easiest to check?
options: Keep four bars even for two repetitions
recall_questions.explanation: A short observable target gives you something concrete to compare.
recall_questions.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
recall_questions.label: Practise one clear target

recall_questions.prompt: Your second attempt is steadier after slowing down. What can you conclude?
recall_questions.explanation: This is evidence about a specific attempt, not proof of general mastery.
recall_questions.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
recall_questions.label: Make and review your own idea

skills.title: Find a steady pulse
skills.subtitle: Keep the beat while the rhythm changes.
skills.deliverable: Tap eight even beats and clap on beats one and three. Notice whether your foot speeds up when the claps change.

lesson.prompt: Your claps change but your foot stays even. What stays consistent?
lesson.explanation: The pulse stays even even when the clapped rhythm changes.
lesson.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
lesson.idea: Keep the beat while the rhythm changes.
lesson.body: A pulse is a regular underlying beat. A rhythm places sounds and silences against it. Tap four even beats first, then clap a pattern while your foot keeps the pulse. Start with counting rather than speed.
lesson.task: Tap eight even beats and clap on beats one and three. Notice whether your foot speeds up when the claps change.

challenges.prompt: What best describes the pulse of a piece?
challenges.explanation: A pulse is the steady timing reference. Rhythms change around it.

content.hint: Think of what your foot taps while music plays.

parallel.prompt: Which part of the music stays even while a clapped pattern changes?
parallel.explanation: The pulse stays even while the rhythm on top of it changes.

challenges.prompt: Build one bar of 4/4, starting from beat 1.
challenges.explanation: Count 1, 2, 3, 4, then return to 1 for the next bar.

parallel.prompt: Count one bar of 3/4, starting from beat 1.
parallel.explanation: A bar of 3/4 counts 1, 2, 3, then returns to 1.

challenges.prompt: Watch four beats, then tap five steady beats.
challenges.explanation: Keep the spaces between taps even. Sumi measures screen taps only; audio is not recorded or graded.

challenges.prompt: Match each idea to its meaning.
challenges.explanation: Pulse is the beat; rhythm is the pattern on top; a rest is counted silence.

right: A silence that still takes time
Sounds and silences placed against the beat

parallel.prompt: Match each word to what it describes.
parallel.explanation: A beat is the pulse; a clap pattern is a rhythm; counted silence is a rest.

skills.title: Watch and apply
skills.subtitle: A short video, then one question that uses it.
skills.deliverable: A short video, then one question that uses it.

challenges.prompt: Watch the pulse video, or read its summary. What stays the same while note lengths change?
challenges.explanation: Linking what you watched to the steady beat helps the next exercise.

content.reference: The video counts a steady beat while longer and shorter notes are placed above it. Notice that the counting never speeds up.

challenges.prompt: In the video, longer notes are added above the count. What happens to the beat?
challenges.explanation: The beat keeps its speed. Longer notes simply span more beats.
options: It stays at the same speed
It slows down to fit them

parallel.prompt: A slow melody plays over a steady count. What does the count do?
parallel.explanation: The count stays even; the melody moves at its own pace above it.

challenges.prompt: Name one moment where you could feel the beat continue through a silence.
challenges.explanation: Noticing counted silence prepares you for rests.

content.task: Write one sentence about where a silence still took time.

skills.title: Give sounds a length
skills.subtitle: Count note values and rests in a simple meter.
skills.deliverable: Write one four-beat bar using note lengths and a rest. Count the silence as carefully as the sounds.

lesson.prompt: How many beats do a half note, a quarter note, and a quarter rest fill in 4/4?
lesson.explanation: Their lengths add to two plus one plus one: four beats.
lesson.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
lesson.idea: Count note values and rests in a simple meter.
lesson.body: For this exercise in 4/4, a quarter note lasts one beat and a half note lasts two. A rest also occupies time. Keep counting during silence so the next sound starts in the right place.
lesson.example:
4/4 bar: half note + quarter note + quarter rest
Beats:       2     +      1       +      1 = 4
lesson.task: Write one four-beat bar using note lengths and a rest. Count the silence as carefully as the sounds.

challenges.prompt: In 4/4 with a quarter-note beat, how long is a half note?
challenges.explanation: A half note lasts two quarter-note beats in this example.

content.hint: A half note fills half of a four-beat bar.

parallel.prompt: In 4/4 with a quarter-note beat, how long is a whole note?
parallel.explanation: A whole note fills the whole four-beat bar.

challenges.prompt: Order these from shortest to longest.
challenges.explanation: Quarter (1 beat) is shorter than half (2 beats), which is shorter than whole (4 beats).

parallel.prompt: Order these rests from shortest to longest.
parallel.explanation: Quarter rest (1 beat), half rest (2 beats), whole rest (4 beats).

challenges.prompt: Match each value to its length in 4/4.
challenges.explanation: Quarter = 1 beat, half = 2 beats, whole = 4 beats when the quarter note gets the beat.

challenges.prompt: A bar has a half note and a quarter note. What fills the last beat?
challenges.explanation: Two beats plus one beat is three; a one-beat rest completes four.

content.hint: Add the beats you already have.

parallel.prompt: A bar has three quarter notes. What completes it?
parallel.explanation: Three beats plus one more beat makes four.

challenges.prompt: Write one four-beat bar using one rest.
challenges.explanation: Counting the rest as carefully as the notes keeps the bar complete.

content.task: Write it with counts, for example: half note (1-2), quarter rest (3), quarter note (4).

skills.title: Shape a small phrase
skills.subtitle: Organize a pattern into bars.
skills.deliverable: Create two bars of counted rhythm. Repeat the first bar, then make one deliberate change in the second.

lesson.prompt: One bar of 4/4 contains only three quarter-note beats so far. What completes it?
lesson.explanation: A one-beat quarter rest brings the bar total to four.
lesson.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
lesson.body: For a first example, use two bars of 4/4. Each bar contains four quarter-note beats. A repeat or a small change can make a short idea recognizable. Keep bar totals correct before adding detail.
lesson.example:
Bar 1: 1  2  3  4 | Bar 2: 1  2  3  4
Idea:  x     x  x |        x  x     x
lesson.task: Create two bars of counted rhythm. Repeat the first bar, then make one deliberate change in the second.

challenges.prompt: How many quarter-note beats fit in two complete bars of 4/4?
challenges.explanation: Each bar has four beats, so two bars hold eight.

content.hint: Four beats per bar, two bars.

parallel.prompt: How many quarter-note beats are in three bars of 4/4?
parallel.explanation: Three bars of four beats give twelve.

challenges.prompt: Put these steps for building a two-bar idea in order.
challenges.explanation: Count a clear first bar, repeat it, then make one deliberate change.

parallel.prompt: Order the steps for checking a new phrase.
options: Check each bar adds to four
parallel.explanation: Write it, check every bar adds up, then perform it.

challenges.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
challenges.explanation: A bar groups beats; the time signature sets how many; a phrase is an idea that spans bars.

right: A short musical idea across bars
How many beats each bar holds

challenges.prompt: Describe your two-bar idea in words.
challenges.explanation: Naming the repeat and the change makes the idea easy to remember.

content.task: Say what repeats and what you changed in bar 2.

challenges.prompt: Your foot taps evenly while your claps change. What is your foot keeping?
challenges.explanation: Even taps keep the pulse while claps make a rhythm.

parallel.prompt: A drummer keeps an even click while a singer changes rhythm. What does the click keep?
parallel.explanation: The click keeps the pulse.

challenges.prompt: Match each note value to its beats in 4/4.
challenges.explanation: Half = 2, quarter rest = 1, whole = 4.

challenges.prompt: One bar of 4/4 has only three beats so far. What completes it?
challenges.explanation: A one-beat rest brings the total to four.

skills.subtitle: New examples. Answer every check correctly to earn a star.
skills.deliverable: New examples. Answer every check correctly to earn a star.

challenges.prompt: A song in 4/4 has a long held note over two beats, then two short sounds. How many beats so far?
challenges.explanation: The held note covers two beats and the two short sounds take one beat each: four.

challenges.prompt: Order a bar of 4/4 that ends with a rest.
challenges.explanation: Beats 1-2 are the half note, beat 3 is the quarter note, beat 4 is the rest.

challenges.prompt: Match each everyday example to the musical idea.
challenges.explanation: Steady ticks are like a pulse; a knock pattern is a rhythm; a timed pause is like a rest.
options: A knock pattern on a door

challenges.prompt: Tap five steady beats at a comfortable speed.
challenges.explanation: Even spacing shows a steady pulse. Screen taps only; audio is not graded.

challenges.prompt: Name one thing you can do now that you could not do at the start of this unit.
challenges.explanation: Noticing your progress helps you choose the next step.

skills.title: Follow a pitch shape
skills.subtitle: Separate high and low from loud and soft.
skills.deliverable: Draw an up-down-up contour, then choose four note names that follow it. Use an instrument if available, or label a paper diagram.

lesson.prompt: A note is played more quietly without changing its frequency. Which property changes?
lesson.explanation: Playing more quietly changes loudness, not the note’s pitch.
lesson.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
lesson.idea: Separate high and low from loud and soft.
lesson.body: Pitch describes how high or low a sound is; loudness is a different property. In the familiar ascending note-letter sequence, C to D to E moves upward. You can first draw that contour without singing or owning an instrument.
lesson.example:
Note names: C → D → E
Contour:    low → higher → higher
lesson.task: Draw an up-down-up contour, then choose four note names that follow it. Use an instrument if available, or label a paper diagram.

challenges.prompt: Which word describes how high or low a note sounds?
challenges.explanation: Pitch is high or low; tempo is speed; duration is length.

content.hint: It is not about speed or volume.

parallel.prompt: A singer moves to a higher note. Which property changed?
parallel.explanation: Moving higher changes pitch.

challenges.prompt: Arrange these note names from low to high.
challenges.explanation: In this register C is lowest, then D, then E.

parallel.prompt: Arrange from low to high.
parallel.explanation: E, then F, then G.

challenges.prompt: Draw an up–down–up contour and label one note name at each turn.
challenges.explanation: A contour drawing records the shape of a melody. Sumi does not grade the drawing.

challenges.prompt: Match each change to the property it affects.
challenges.explanation: Quieter changes loudness; C to E changes pitch; holding changes duration.

parallel.prompt: A note moves down the staff. What happens to its pitch?

challenges.prompt: Describe the shape of a melody you know: does it start by going up or down?

lesson.prompt: What best supports a useful practice reflection?
options: A specific observation about one attempt
lesson.explanation: A specific observation suggests a practical next adjustment.
lesson.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
lesson.body: Set a small observable target, such as keeping a pattern even for two repetitions. Choose a speed at which you can do that comfortably. Isolate the difficult section and repeat it before joining the full phrase. A slower clean version is useful evidence.
lesson.example:
Target: two even repetitions
Observe: where did the pulse change?
Adjust: slow down and isolate that point
lesson.task: Try your two-bar pattern twice. Record one specific difficulty and one change you made. The app does not listen or automatically score your performance.

content.hint: Which choice gives you more time to notice what happens?

parallel.prompt: You keep stumbling on bar 3. What should you practise?
parallel.explanation: Isolating the difficult bar at a slower speed targets the problem.

challenges.prompt: Put this practice loop in order.
challenges.explanation: Set a target, try it, notice what happened, then adjust one thing.

challenges.prompt: Tap five steady beats slowly, as if practising carefully.

options: Bar three rushed; repeat it more slowly
lesson.explanation: It identifies a location, an observable issue, and a concrete practice step.

lesson.body: Make a short original pattern using ideas you can explain. Count each bar, perform it twice, and compare the attempts. A recording can help you notice timing, but the review is yours: this prototype does not judge audio or musical expression.
lesson.example: Create → count → perform → compare → change one thing
lesson.task: Make an original four-bar rhythm, mark one rest, and write a two-sentence review of its timing. Use paper, clapping, or an instrument.

parallel.prompt: Before sharing a new 3/4 rhythm, what should each bar total?

challenges.prompt: Make an original four-bar rhythm and review it.

A phrase is a short idea across bars: repeat, then change one thing.

lesson.prompt: Which comparison is useful when choosing fabric for a structured item?
lesson.explanation: These properties affect how the item holds its shape and can be constructed.
lesson.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
lesson.body: Fabric choice changes how an item hangs and holds a seam. Compare the stretch and feel of a woven and a knit if you have scraps. On woven fabric, the lengthwise grain runs parallel to the selvage. Follow a pattern’s grainline and fabric recommendations rather than treating every material alike.
lesson.example:
Woven fabric: selvage ║ lengthwise grain
Compare: stretch, thickness, drape, fraying
lesson.task: Compare two fabric scraps or written fabric descriptions. Record stretch, thickness, and whether the edge frays. Explain which suits your brief.

skills.title: Measure with a clear record
skills.subtitle: Use consistent units and repeat checks.
skills.deliverable: Measure a notebook or paper rectangle twice. Label width, height, and units. Compare the two readings before planning a pattern.

lesson.prompt: Your two width measurements differ. What is a useful next step?
lesson.explanation: Checking the method and repeating the measurement can reveal the source of the difference.
lesson.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
lesson.idea: Use consistent units and repeat checks.
lesson.body: Record what was measured, the units, and any intended ease or allowance separately. Repeat a measurement before cutting. A measurement is not a pattern size by itself; compare it with the specific pattern’s sizing information. For this demo, practise on paper or an object rather than entering personal body measurements.
lesson.example:
Object width: 12 cm
Object height: 18 cm
Allowances: recorded separately
lesson.task: Measure a notebook or paper rectangle twice. Label width, height, and units. Compare the two readings before planning a pattern.

skills.title: Separate stitching from cutting
skills.subtitle: Add the specified seam allowance.
skills.deliverable: Draw an 8 × 10 cm finished rectangle on paper. Add a separate 1 cm seam allowance on every edge, then label both lines.

lesson.prompt: A finished width is 8 cm with 1 cm allowance at both sides. What is the cut width?
lesson.explanation: The two allowances add two centimeters to the finished width.
lesson.hint: Break the idea into one small step.
lesson.body: A stitch line marks where pieces join. A cut line may include extra fabric outside it. That extra width is the seam allowance. Follow the allowance stated by the pattern; not every pattern uses the same value. Practise with a paper rectangle before using fabric.
lesson.example:
Finished rectangle: 8 × 10 cm
Allowance: 1 cm on every edge
Cut rectangle: 10 × 12 cm
lesson.task: Draw an 8 × 10 cm finished rectangle on paper. Add a separate 1 cm seam allowance on every edge, then label both lines.

challenges.prompt: What is a seam allowance?
challenges.explanation: It is the width outside the stitching line used to join pieces.
options: Extra fabric between the stitch line and the cut edge

content.hint: It sits between two lines on the pattern.

parallel.prompt: On a pattern piece, what is between the stitch line and the cut line?
parallel.explanation: That margin is the seam allowance.

challenges.prompt: A finished width is 12 cm with 1 cm allowance each side. What is the cut width?
challenges.explanation: Add 1 cm on the left and 1 cm on the right: 14 cm.

parallel.prompt: A finished width is 8 cm with 1.5 cm allowance each side. What is the cut width?
parallel.explanation: Add 1.5 cm twice: 11 cm.

lesson.idea: Review the result against the brief.
lesson.body: Choose an edge finish that suits the material and use. Check for loose stitches, fraying, and uneven edges. Pressing and care depend on the fabric, so use its care instructions and test scraps first. Finally compare the item or mockup with your original brief and name one improvement.

Review: function + dimensions + secure join + clean edge
Improve: one observable change at a time
